steps.prompt: Same letters, different meaning. What changes?
steps.a: I helped my uncle Jack off a horse.
steps.b: I helped my uncle jack off a horse.
steps.reveal: In A, Uncle Jack is a person getting off a horse. In B, “jack” is a verb, and it sounds like your uncle is using a car jack to lift a horse! One capital letter tells the reader which words are names.

cards.title: Always a capital
cards.body: The first word of every sentence. The word I (and I’m, I’ve, I’ll). Names of people and pets (Maya, Rex). Titles before a name (Mr. Diaz, Dr. Lee, Aunt Rosa).

cards.title: Names of places and things
cards.text:
Places: Chicago, Lake Michigan, Main Street, Canada
Days, months and holidays: Tuesday, March, Thanksgiving
Languages and nationalities: English, Spanish, Mexican
Titles: The Hunger Games, “Happy Birthday”
cards.note: In titles, capitalise the first word and the important words. Little words (a, the, of, and, in) stay small unless they come first.

cards.title: No capital needed
cards.telling: In the Summer, my Mom took a Science class.
cards.showing: In the summer, my mom took a science class.
cards.note: Seasons and most school subjects are ordinary nouns. “mom” after my/your/his is a common noun; “Mom” on its own is used as a name: “Mom, where are my shoes?”

cards.title: The name test
cards.body: Ask: is this the name of one particular person, place or thing? Then it needs a capital: a river → the Amazon River; my school → Lincoln Middle School.

prompts: Which capital letter rule surprised you the most?
Think of your own writing. Do you add capitals where they don’t belong, or forget them where they do?
